theory.title: Why this lesson?
theory.body: Circuit problems mix very large and very small numbers: a resistor of $5\ \text{k}\Omega$, a current of $6\ \text{mA}$, a capacitor of $10\ \mu\text{F}$. Before Lecture 1 you should be able to convert such values quickly and without mistakes. **This lesson is an addition for beginners — it is not part of the course presentations.**

theory.title: The main electrical quantities and their SI units
theory.body:
| Quantity | Symbol | Unit | Unit symbol |
|---|---|---|---|
| charge | $q$, $Q$ | coulomb | C |
| current | $i$, $I$ | ampere | A |
| voltage | $v$, $V$ | volt | V |
| resistance | $R$ | ohm | Ω |
| conductance | $G$ | siemens | S |
| power | $p$, $P$ | watt | W |
| energy | $w$, $W$ | joule | J |
| capacitance | $C$ | farad | F |
| inductance | $L$ | henry | H |

Lower-case letters ($v$, $i$, $p$) usually denote quantities that may change with time; capitals ($V$, $I$) denote constant (DC) values.

theory.title: SI prefixes used most often in circuits
theory.body:
giga G $=10^{9}$, mega M $=10^{6}$, kilo k $=10^{3}$, milli m $=10^{-3}$, micro μ $=10^{-6}$, nano n $=10^{-9}$, pico p $=10^{-12}$.

**How to convert:** replace the prefix by its power of ten. $4.7\ \text{k}\Omega = 4.7\times10^{3}\ \Omega = 4700\ \Omega$; $250\ \text{mA} = 250\times10^{-3}\ \text{A} = 0.25\ \text{A}$.

**Watch out:** «m» (milli, $10^{-3}$) and «M» (mega, $10^{6}$) differ only in the letter case.

theory.title: Working with powers of ten
theory.body:
- Multiplication adds exponents: $10^{3}\cdot10^{-3} = 10^{0} = 1$. So $V = IR = (2\ \text{mA})(5\ \text{k}\Omega) = 10\ \text{V}$ — milli and kilo cancel.
- Division subtracts exponents: $\frac{30\ \text{V}}{5\ \text{k}\Omega} = 6\times10^{-3}\ \text{A} = 6\ \text{mA}$.
- Squaring doubles the exponent: $(6\ \text{mA})^2 = 36\times10^{-6}\ \text{A}^2$.

theory.title: Why this lesson?
theory.body: Every problem in this course starts with a schematic. You must recognise each symbol and understand what the «+», «−» signs and the arrows mean before you can write a single equation. **This lesson is an addition for beginners — it is not part of the course presentations.**

theory.title: Common symbols
theory.body:
| Symbol in the lectures | Element |
|---|---|
| zig-zag line | resistor $R$ |
| circle with «+» and «−» | independent voltage source (the «+» terminal is at the higher potential) |
| circle with an arrow | independent current source (the arrow shows the direction of its current) |
| diamond with «+», «−» | dependent (controlled) voltage source |
| diamond with an arrow | dependent (controlled) current source |
| long and short parallel lines | battery: **the longer line is the positive terminal** |
| horizontal lines / downward arrow at a node | reference node (ground), $v = 0$ |
| two parallel plates | capacitor $C$ |
| coil | inductor $L$ |
| triangle with «+» and «−» inputs | operational amplifier |

theory.title: Reference directions and polarities
theory.body:
- A current arrow is only a **reference direction**. You may choose it freely; if the calculated current is negative, the real current flows the other way (Lecture 3 uses this, e.g. $i_2 = -1.67$ A).
- A pair «+ / −» next to an element is the **reference polarity** of its voltage: $v$ is the potential of the «+» end minus the potential of the «−» end.
- Some exercise sheets (PS04, PS05) mark a voltage with a curved arrow instead of «+ / −»; the arrow points towards the terminal taken as «+».
- Conventional current flows from higher to lower potential through a resistor, i.e. opposite to the motion of electrons in a wire.

theory.title: Nodes are wires, not dots
theory.body: All points joined by ideal wires (zero resistance) form **one node** and have the same potential, even if the drawing places them far apart or bends the wire. Before analysing a circuit, colour each node: this immediately shows which elements are in parallel (same pair of nodes) and which are in series (a node shared by only two elements).

theory.title: Why this lesson?
theory.body: Lecture 3 turns a circuit into a system of linear equations; Lecture 6 uses derivatives ($i = C\,dv/dt$) and integrals ($v = \frac1C\int i\,dt$). This lesson recalls only what is needed. **It is an addition for beginners — not part of the presentations.**

theory.title: Solving two linear equations by substitution
theory.body:
Example: $3v_1 - v_2 = 20$ and $-3v_1 + 5v_2 = 60$.
1. Add the equations: $4v_2 = 80 \Rightarrow v_2 = 20$.
2. Substitute back: $3v_1 = 20 + 20 \Rightarrow v_1 = 13.33$.
Always check: $-3(13.33) + 5(20) = 60$ ✓. (Lecture 3 solves the same system with Cramer's rule — the result is identical.)

theory.title: Determinant of a 2×2 matrix and Cramer's rule
theory.body: For $\begin{cases}ax + by = e\\ cx + dy = f\end{cases}$: $\Delta = ad - bc$. If $\Delta \ne 0$: $x = \frac{ed - bf}{\Delta}$, $y = \frac{af - ec}{\Delta}$. For the example above: $\Delta = 3\cdot5 - (-1)(-3) = 12$, $v_1 = \frac{20\cdot5 - (-1)\cdot60}{12} = \frac{160}{12} = 13.33$.

theory.title: Derivative = rate of change, integral = accumulated area
theory.body:
- $\frac{dv}{dt}$ is the **slope** of the graph $v(t)$: how fast $v$ changes. If $v$ rises linearly by $10$ V in $2$ s, $\frac{dv}{dt} = 5$ V/s. If $v$ is constant, $\frac{dv}{dt} = 0$.
- $\int_{t_1}^{t_2} i\,dt$ is the **area** under the graph $i(t)$ between $t_1$ and $t_2$. A constant current of $3$ A during $4$ s carries $Q = 3\cdot4 = 12$ C.
These two ideas are enough for the capacitor and inductor problems of Lecture 6, where the graphs are made of straight-line pieces.

theory.title: What does electricity mean?
theory.body:
All materials are made of atoms (protons, neutrons, electrons). Without a voltage, the free electrons of a conductor move randomly. When a voltage is applied, they drift in one direction — this directional motion of charges is the **electric current**.

A higher voltage difference is like a higher height difference in a water system: it causes a stronger flow. So: the battery creates a voltage, the voltage makes the electrons move, and the motion of the electrons is the current.

theory.title: Electric circuit
theory.body: An **electric circuit** is an interconnection of electrical elements. A basic circuit consists of a battery (the source of electricity), electrical loads, and wires connecting them.

theory.title: Electric charge
theory.body:
**Charge** is an electrical property of the atomic particles of which matter consists, measured in **coulombs (C)**. The charge of the electron is negative and equal in magnitude to $e = 1.602\times10^{-19}$ C. Realistic (laboratory) values of charge are of the order of pC or nC.

Electric charge ($Q$) is a property of matter; electrons carry negative charge; the motion of electric charges forms the electric current ($I$).

theory.title: Electric current
theory.body:
**Electric current** is the time rate of change of charge — the rate at which charge flows through a conductor — measured in **amperes (A)**:
$i = \frac{dq}{dt}$, $\quad 1\ \text{A} = 1\ \text{C/s}$.

The total charge transferred between $t_0$ and $t$ is the integral of the current: $Q = \int_{t_0}^{t} i\,dt$ («how much charge flows through a conductor during a given period of time»).

theory.title: Direction of the current (addition)
theory.body: The slides ask «What is the direction of the electric current?» (L1·10). In circuit analysis the **conventional current** is used: its direction is the direction in which **positive** charge would move — from the higher potential to the lower one through a resistor. In a metal wire the electrons actually move the other way, so conventional current is opposite to the electron flow. All formulas and arrows in this course use conventional current.

theory.title: Types of current
theory.body: **Direct current (DC)** remains constant with time. **Alternating current (AC)** varies sinusoidally with time.

theory.title: System of units
theory.body: The course uses SI: length — metre (m), mass — kilogram (kg), time — second (s), electric current — ampere (A), thermodynamic temperature — kelvin (K), luminous intensity — candela (cd); the derived unit of charge is the coulomb (C). Prefixes from exa ($10^{18}$) to atto ($10^{-18}$) scale the units (Table 1.2 on the slide).

theory.title: Voltage
theory.body:
Moving electrons in a conductor in a particular direction requires work (energy transfer). This work is done by an external **electromotive force (emf)**, typically a battery.

The **voltage** $v_{ab}$ between points $a$ and $b$ is the energy (work) needed to move a unit charge from $a$ to $b$:
$v_{ab} = \frac{dw}{dq}$, $\quad 1\ \text{V} = 1\ \text{J/C} = 1\ \text{N·m/C}$.

Voltage (potential difference) is measured in volts (V).

theory.title: Water analogy
theory.body: A DC circuit compares to a water loop: the voltage source is the pump (it creates the pressure difference), the electron flow is the water flow, the light bulb is the turbine. A higher pump pressure (voltage) gives a stronger flow (current).

theory.title: Polarity
theory.body: The «+» and «−» signs define the reference polarity. A voltage of $9$ V with «+» at $a$ means that $a$ is $9$ V above $b$. The same voltage can be written as $-9$ V with «+» at $b$: $b$ is $-9$ V above $a$. In general $v_{ab} = -v_{ba}$.

theory.title: Why power and energy?
theory.body: Current and voltage alone are not sufficient: we need to know how much power a device can handle (a 100-W bulb gives more light than a 60-W bulb), and electric bills charge for the energy consumed over a period.

theory.title: Power
theory.body: **Power** is the rate at which work is done, measured in watts (W): $p = \frac{dw}{dt} = \frac{dw}{dq}\cdot\frac{dq}{dt} = vi$. One watt is one joule of work done in one second.

theory.title: Passive sign convention
theory.body:
The **passive sign convention** is satisfied when the current enters through the **positive** terminal of an element; then $p = +vi$. If the current enters through the negative terminal, $p = -vi$.

$p > 0$: the element **absorbs** power; $p < 0$: it **supplies** power. «+ power absorbed = − power supplied».

theory.title: Conservation of energy
theory.body: The algebraic sum of the powers in a circuit, at any instant of time, must be zero: $\sum p = 0$. The total power supplied equals the total power absorbed.

theory.title: Energy
theory.body: **Energy** is the capacity to do work, measured in joules (J) or watt-seconds: $w = \int_{t_0}^{t} p\,dt = \int_{t_0}^{t} vi\,dt$. Electric utilities measure energy in watt-hours: $1\ \text{Wh} = 3600$ J.

theory.title: Passive and active elements
theory.body: Elements of electric circuits are **passive** or **active**. An active element can generate energy, a passive element cannot. Passive: resistors, capacitors, inductors. Active: generators, batteries, operational amplifiers.

theory.title: Independent source
theory.body: An ideal **independent source** is an active element that provides a specified voltage or current that is completely independent of other circuit elements. It is drawn as a circle: with «+ / −» for a voltage source, with an arrow for a current source.

theory.title: Dependent (controlled) source
Resistance and resistivity
theory.body:
**Resistance** is the ability of a material to resist current, symbol $R$, measured in ohms (Ω). For a uniform conductor of length $L$ and cross-sectional area $A$:
$R = \rho\frac{L}{A}$,
where $\rho$ is the **resistivity** in Ω·m. Good conductors (copper $1.72\times10^{-8}$, aluminium $2.8\times10^{-8}$ Ω·m) have low resistivity; insulators (paper $10^{10}$, glass $10^{12}$ Ω·m) have high resistivity; semiconductors (carbon, germanium, silicon) are in between.

theory.title: Fixed and variable, linear and nonlinear resistors
theory.body: Resistors can be fixed or variable (potentiometer). A **linear** resistor obeys Ohm's law: constant resistance, the $i$–$v$ graph is a straight line through the origin. A **nonlinear** resistor does not obey Ohm's law: its resistance varies with the current.

theory.title: Ohm's law
theory.body: The voltage $v$ across a resistor is directly proportional to the current $i$ flowing through it: $v = iR$ (current entering the «+» terminal). The constant of proportionality $R$ is the resistance.

theory.title: Short circuit and open circuit
theory.body: A **short circuit** is an element with resistance approaching zero ($v = 0$ for any current). An **open circuit** is an element with resistance approaching infinity ($i = 0$ for any voltage).

theory.title: Conductance
theory.body: **Conductance** is the ability of an element to conduct current, the reciprocal of resistance: $G = \frac1R = \frac iv$, measured in siemens (S) or mho (℧). The power dissipated by a resistor: $p = vi = i^2R = \frac{v^2}{R} = v^2G = \frac{i^2}{G}$.

theory.title: Branch, node, loop
theory.body: A **branch** represents a single element (a voltage source, a resistor…). A **node** is the point of connection between two or more branches. A **loop** is any closed path in a circuit.

theory.title: Series and parallel connection
theory.body: Two or more elements are in **series** if they exclusively share a single node and consequently carry the **same current**. They are in **parallel** if they are connected to the same two nodes and consequently have the **same voltage** across them.

theory.title: Kirchhoff's current law (KCL)
theory.body:
KCL is based on the conservation of charge: the algebraic sum of the currents entering a node (or a closed boundary) is zero. Equivalently, **the sum of the currents entering a node equals the sum of the currents leaving it**.

Example (slide L2·16): three current sources $I_1$ (up), $I_2$ (down), $I_3$ (up) feed node $a$, from which $I_T$ leaves: $I_T + I_2 = I_1 + I_3$, i.e. $I_T = I_1 - I_2 + I_3$.

theory.title: Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL)
theory.body:
The algebraic sum of all voltages around a closed path (loop) is zero: **sum of voltage drops = sum of voltage rises**.

A voltage **drop** means the potential decreases as you move across the element; a **rise** means it increases. They are not different types of voltage — the same voltage described with a direction.

theory.title: How to write KVL (sign rule used in the examples)
theory.body: Go around the loop in a chosen direction. For each element write $+v$ if you enter it at its «+» terminal and $-v$ if you enter at its «−» terminal. Example (L2·18): $-20 + v_1 - v_2 = 0$.

theory.title: Series resistors and voltage division
theory.body:
The equivalent resistance of resistors in series is the sum: $R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2 + \dots + R_N$.

**Voltage divider:** a voltage $v$ across series resistors divides in proportion to the resistances: $v_n = \frac{R_n}{R_1 + R_2 + \dots + R_N}\,v$; for two resistors $v_1 = \frac{R_1}{R_1+R_2}v$, $v_2 = \frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}v$.

theory.title: Parallel resistors and current division
theory.body:
For two resistors in parallel: $R_{eq} = \frac{R_1R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$ (product over sum). For $N$ resistors: $\frac{1}{R_{eq}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \dots + \frac{1}{R_N}$. $R_{eq}$ is always smaller than the smallest resistor; for $N$ equal resistors $R_{eq} = R/N$.

**Current divider:** $i_1 = \frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}\,i$, $i_2 = \frac{R_1}{R_1+R_2}\,i$ — the larger current flows through the smaller resistor.

theory.title: Conductance form
theory.body: With conductances the roles swap: parallel — $G_{eq} = G_1 + G_2 + \dots + G_N$; series — $\frac{1}{G_{eq}} = \frac{1}{G_1} + \dots + \frac{1}{G_N}$; current division $i_1 = \frac{G_1}{G_1+G_2}\,i$.

theory.title: Shorted and open resistors
theory.body: A resistor in parallel with a short circuit ($R_2 = 0$) carries no current: all current goes through the short. A resistor in series with an open circuit ($R_2 = \infty$) carries no current either; in parallel with an open circuit it takes the whole current.

theory.title: Reduction step by step
theory.body: «Solution by reduction»: combine the resistors that are clearly in series or in parallel, redraw, and repeat until one equivalent resistor remains. Then go back through the drawings using voltage and current division to find the requested quantities.

theory.title: Wye and delta connections
theory.body: Sometimes resistors are neither in series nor in parallel. Three resistors joined at a common node $n$ form a **wye (Y, star, T)** network; three resistors forming a triangle between three terminals form a **delta (Δ, pi)** network.

theory.title: Delta → wye
theory.body: $R_1 = \frac{R_bR_c}{R_a+R_b+R_c}$, $R_2 = \frac{R_cR_a}{R_a+R_b+R_c}$, $R_3 = \frac{R_aR_b}{R_a+R_b+R_c}$. Each Y resistor is the product of the two adjacent Δ resistors divided by the sum of the three Δ resistors.

theory.title: Wye → delta
theory.body: $R_a = \frac{R_1R_2+R_2R_3+R_3R_1}{R_1}$, $R_b = \frac{R_1R_2+R_2R_3+R_3R_1}{R_2}$, $R_c = \frac{R_1R_2+R_2R_3+R_3R_1}{R_3}$. Each Δ resistor is the sum of all products of Y resistors taken two at a time divided by the opposite Y resistor.

theory.title: Balanced networks
theory.body: If $R_1 = R_2 = R_3 = R_Y$ and $R_a = R_b = R_c = R_\Delta$ (balanced), then $R_Y = \frac{R_\Delta}{3}$, $R_\Delta = 3R_Y$.

theory.title: Resistors as models of devices
theory.body: Resistors model devices that convert electrical energy into heat or other forms of energy: wires, light bulbs, electric heaters, ovens, loudspeakers. Light bulbs may be connected in **parallel** (each bulb gets the full supply voltage; one failing bulb does not switch off the others) or in **series** (one current through all bulbs).

theory.title: Two general methods
theory.body: Using Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws we now build two powerful techniques: **nodal analysis**, based on KCL, and **mesh analysis**, based on KVL. Any linear circuit can be analysed by writing a set of simultaneous equations and solving them for the unknown voltages or currents. This part should be regarded as the most important in the course.

theory.title: Steps of nodal analysis
theory.body:
Nodal analysis uses **node voltages** as circuit variables: this reduces the number of simultaneous equations.
1. Select a node as the **reference node** (ground, $v = 0$). Assign voltages $v_1, v_2, \dots, v_{n-1}$ to the remaining $n - 1$ nodes; they are measured with respect to the reference.
2. Apply **KCL** to each of the $n - 1$ non-reference nodes. Use Ohm's law to express the branch currents in terms of node voltages: current from node $a$ to node $b$ through $R$ is $\frac{v_a - v_b}{R}$.
3. Solve the resulting simultaneous equations.

theory.title: The reference node
theory.body: Common symbols for the reference node: (a) common ground, (b) ground, (c) chassis ground. The choice is free; a node with many connections (often the bottom wire) gives the simplest equations.

theory.title: Example of the equations
theory.body:
For the circuit with $I_1$, $I_2$, $R_1$, $R_2$, $R_3$ (slides L3·7–9):
node 1: $I_1 = I_2 + i_1 + i_2$; node 2: $I_2 + i_2 = i_3$, with $i_1 = \frac{v_1}{R_1} = G_1v_1$, $i_2 = \frac{v_1 - v_2}{R_2} = G_2(v_1 - v_2)$, $i_3 = \frac{v_2}{R_3} = G_3v_2$.
In matrix form: $\begin{bmatrix}G_1+G_2 & -G_2\\ -G_2 & G_2+G_3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}v_1\\ v_2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}I_1 - I_2\\ I_2\end{bmatrix}$.

theory.title: Cramer's rule
theory.body:
For $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ with $\det A \ne 0$ the system has exactly one solution: $x_k = \frac{\Delta_k}{\Delta}$, where $\Delta = \det A$ and $\Delta_k$ is the determinant of $A$ with column $k$ replaced by $\mathbf{b}$.
- 2×2: $\det\begin{bmatrix}a & b\\ c & d\end{bmatrix} = ad - bc$; $x = \frac{ed - bf}{\Delta}$, $y = \frac{af - ce}{\Delta}$ for $ax + by = e$, $cx + dy = f$.
- 3×3: expand along the first row, $\det A = a_1(b_2c_3 - b_3c_2) - a_2(b_1c_3 - b_3c_1) + a_3(b_1c_2 - b_2c_1)$, or use the diagonal (Sarrus) rule.
If the determinant is 0, the matrix has no inverse.

theory.title: Two cases
theory.body:
**Case 1:** a voltage source is connected between the reference node and a non-reference node — simply set the node voltage equal to the source voltage (e.g. $v_1 = 10$ V).

**Case 2:** a voltage source (dependent or independent) is connected between two non-reference nodes — the two nodes form a **generalized node or supernode**. Apply both KCL and KVL to determine the node voltages.

theory.title: Supernode
theory.body: A **supernode** is formed by enclosing a (dependent or independent) voltage source connected between two non-reference nodes and any elements connected in parallel with it. KCL is written for the whole supernode (sum of currents leaving the closed surface $= 0$), and KVL across the source gives the extra equation, e.g. $-v_2 + 5 + v_3 = 0 \Rightarrow v_2 - v_3 = 5$.

theory.title: Why nodal analysis?
theory.body: It simplifies complex circuits (we solve for node voltages instead of many currents); it works well with many components, especially current sources; a circuit with $N$ nodes needs only $N - 1$ equations; once node voltages are known, every current follows from Ohm's law.

theory.title: Mesh
theory.body: Mesh analysis (loop analysis) uses **mesh currents** as circuit variables and is based on KVL. A **mesh** is the smallest closed loop in a circuit that does not contain another loop inside it. It reduces the number of equations that must be solved simultaneously. It applies to **planar** circuits.

theory.title: Steps of mesh analysis
theory.body:
1. Identify all meshes in the circuit.
2. Assign a mesh current (usually clockwise) to each mesh.
3. Apply KVL around each mesh.
4. Use Ohm's law $V = IR$ to express voltages; a resistor shared by meshes 1 and 2 carries $i_1 - i_2$ (seen from mesh 1).
5. Solve the equations for the mesh currents; branch currents follow (e.g. $I_3 = i_1 - i_2$).

theory.title: Case 1 — current source in one mesh only
theory.body: The mesh current equals the source current. Example: $i_2 = -5$ A, then KVL for the other mesh: $-10 + 4i_1 + 6(i_1 - i_2) = 0 \Rightarrow i_1 = -2$ A.

theory.title: Case 2 — current source between two meshes (supermesh)
theory.body:
Create a **supermesh** by excluding the current source and any elements connected in series with it; write KVL around the supermesh. A supermesh results when two meshes have a (dependent or independent) current source in common.

Properties: 1) the current source provides the constraint equation (KCL at a node of the shared branch); 2) a supermesh has no current of its own; 3) it requires both KVL and KCL.

theory.title: Choosing the method
theory.body:
- Many series elements, voltage sources or supermeshes → **mesh analysis**.
- Many parallel elements, current sources or supernodes → **nodal analysis**.
- Fewer nodes than meshes → nodal; fewer meshes than nodes → mesh. The key is the **smallest number of equations**.
- If node voltages are required → nodal; if branch or mesh currents are required → mesh may be better.
- For **nonplanar** networks nodal analysis is the only option (mesh analysis applies only to planar networks). Nodal analysis is easily programmed on computers.

theory.title: Why circuit theorems?
theory.body: Kirchhoff's laws, nodal and mesh analysis are enough for simple circuits. For large and complex circuits other tools help: **superposition, source transformation, Thevenin's and Norton's theorems**.

theory.title: Superposition principle
theory.body: In a **linear** circuit with two or more independent sources, the voltage across (or current through) an element is the **algebraic sum** of the voltages (currents) due to each independent source acting alone.

theory.title: How to turn sources off
theory.body:
Consider one independent source at a time; all other **independent** sources are turned off:
- a voltage source is replaced by $0$ V — a **short circuit**;
- a current source is replaced by $0$ A — an **open circuit**.
**Dependent sources are left intact**: they are controlled by circuit variables. Disadvantage: superposition may involve more work than a single nodal/mesh analysis.

theory.title: Steps
theory.body:
1. Turn off all independent sources except one.
2. Find the output (voltage or current) due to that source using the previous techniques.
3. Repeat for each of the other independent sources.
4. Add all the contributions algebraically.

theory.title: Superposition does not apply to power
theory.body: Power is not linear ($p = i^2R$): find the total current or voltage by superposition first, then compute the power. Adding the powers of the separate contributions gives a wrong result.

theory.title: Source transformation
theory.body:
A **source transformation** replaces a voltage source $v_s$ in series with a resistor $R$ by a current source $i_s$ in parallel with the same $R$, or vice versa:
$v_s = i_sR \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad i_s = \frac{v_s}{R}$.
Both networks give the same voltage and current at terminals $a$–$b$. Like series–parallel combination and Δ–Y transformation, it is a tool for simplifying circuits.

theory.title: Notes
theory.body:
1. The arrow of the current source is directed **toward the positive terminal** of the voltage source.
2. Transformation is not possible when $R = 0$ (ideal voltage source) or $R = \infty$ (ideal current source).
3. It also works for dependent sources, as long as the controlling variable stays in the circuit.

theory.title: Motivation
theory.body: Often one element (the **load**) is variable while the rest is fixed — e.g. a household outlet with different appliances. Re-analysing the whole circuit for every load is wasteful; Thevenin's theorem replaces the fixed part by a simple equivalent circuit.

theory.title: Thevenin's theorem
Finding $R_{Th}$
theory.body:
**Case 1 — no dependent sources:** turn off all independent sources; $R_{Th}$ is the input resistance seen from $a$–$b$.

**Case 2 — dependent sources present:** turn off the independent sources (dependent ones stay), apply a test voltage $v_o$ (or test current $i_o$) at $a$–$b$ and compute the other quantity: $R_{Th} = \frac{v_o}{i_o}$. Any value can be assumed ($v_o = 1$ V or $i_o = 1$ A). $R_{Th}$ may come out negative: the circuit then supplies power ($v = -iR$).

theory.title: Load current and voltage
theory.body: With the Thevenin equivalent: $I_L = \frac{V_{Th}}{R_{Th} + R_L}$, $V_L = R_LI_L = \frac{R_L}{R_{Th} + R_L}V_{Th}$.

theory.title: Norton's theorem
Thevenin–Norton transformation
theory.body: $R_N = R_{Th}$ and $I_N = \frac{V_{Th}}{R_{Th}}$ — the Norton equivalent is the source transformation of the Thevenin equivalent. Any two of $v_{oc}$, $i_{sc}$, $R_{Th}$ determine the third: $R_{Th} = \frac{v_{oc}}{i_{sc}}$.

theory.title: Maximum power transfer
theory.body:
A circuit is often designed to deliver power to a load (e.g. in communications). With the Thevenin equivalent, the load power is
$p = i^2R_L = \left(\frac{V_{Th}}{R_{Th} + R_L}\right)^2 R_L$.
**Maximum power is transferred when the load resistance equals the Thevenin resistance: $R_L = R_{Th}$.** Then $p_{\max} = \frac{V_{Th}^2}{4R_{Th}}$.

theory.title: Proof
theory.body: Differentiate $p$ with respect to $R_L$: $\frac{dp}{dR_L} = V_{Th}^2\left[\frac{(R_{Th}+R_L)^2 - 2R_L(R_{Th}+R_L)}{(R_{Th}+R_L)^4}\right] = V_{Th}^2\frac{R_{Th} - R_L}{(R_{Th}+R_L)^3} = 0 \Rightarrow R_L = R_{Th}$.

theory.title: The operational amplifier
theory.body: The **op-amp** is an electronic device composed of a large number of electronic elements (e.g. the μA741 in an 8-pin package: inverting input, non-inverting input, output, supply pins $\pm V_{dc}$, offset null). It is useful for real applications (amplifiers). In this course we analyse circuits with op-amps using **idealized models**, defined by the behaviour at the external terminals, not by the internal structure.

theory.title: External terminals
theory.body: Non-inverting input ($v^+$, current $i^+$), inverting input ($v^-$, current $i^-$), output ($v_o$, current $i_o$), and the reference terminal («ground»). The **differential input voltage** is $v_d = v^+ - v^-$. Usually the ground terminal is not part of the symbol: it is provided externally by the power-supply network (the midpoint of the $\pm V_{dc}$ supplies).

theory.title: Experimental model
theory.body:
Model: input resistance $R_i$ between the inputs, output resistance $R_o$ in series with a dependent source $Av_d = A(v^+ - v^-)$. Typical values (μA741): $R_i = 2$ MΩ, $R_o = 75\ \Omega$, open-loop gain $A = 200\,000$ (between $10^5$ and $10^6$).

Simplified: $v_o = Av_d$, $i^+ = i^- = 0$. The transfer characteristic is linear only for $|v_d| < v_{d\max} = V_{sat}/A$; outside, the output **saturates** at $\pm V_{sat}$ (slightly below $\pm V_{dc}$).

theory.title: Inverting amplifier with the experimental model
theory.body:
With $R_i$ (input resistor) and $R_f$ (feedback resistor), solving the circuit with $\hat e = Av_d$:
$v_d = -v_i\frac{R_f}{R_f + (1+A)R_i}$, $\quad G = \frac{v_o}{v_i} = -\frac{AR_f}{R_f + (1+A)R_i}$.

theory.title: The ideal op-amp
theory.body:
For $A \to \infty$: $v_d \to 0$ and $G \to -\frac{R_f}{R_i}$ (gain of the inverting amplifier). **Ideal op-amp characteristic:**
$i^+ = 0$, $i^- = 0$, $v_d = 0$ (the inputs are at the same potential — «virtual short»).
Validity conditions: $|v_o| < V_{sat}$ and $|i_o| < I_{sat}$.

theory.title: General method
theory.body: Write KVL/KCL together with the ideal op-amp constitutive relations $i^+ = i^- = 0$, $v_d = 0$.

theory.title: Inverting amplifier with the ideal model
theory.body:
- KCL at the inverting input: $I - I_f - i^- = 0 \Rightarrow I_f = I$.
- KVL around the input loop: $v_i - R_iI + v_d = 0 \Rightarrow I = \frac{v_i}{R_i}$.
- KVL around the output loop: $v_o + R_fI + v_d = 0 \Rightarrow v_o = -R_fI = -\frac{R_f}{R_i}v_i$.

theory.title: Remarks
theory.body:
- The output voltage does not depend on the load: the op-amp stage behaves as an **independent voltage source**.
- The op-amp output current is found a posteriori by KCL at the output node: $I_o = I_L - I_f = \frac{v_o}{R_L} - \frac{v_i}{R_i}$. **The output current $I_o$ is NOT zero.**

theory.title: Nodal analysis with an ideal op-amp
theory.body:
- Only two of the three op-amp node voltages are independent: $e_+ - e_- = 0$ and the output $e_k$ — the number of unknowns drops from 3 to 2.
- The output behaves as a VCVS and gives no information on its current: **do not write KCL at the output node of the op-amp.**

theory.title: Inverting stage
theory.body: $v_o = -\frac{R_f}{R_i}v_i$. The non-inverting input is grounded; the inverting input is a «virtual ground».

theory.title: Non-inverting stage
theory.body: The input goes to the non-inverting terminal; $R$ connects the inverting input to ground and $R_f$ goes from the output to the inverting input: $\frac{v_o}{v_i} = \frac{R + R_f}{R} = 1 + \frac{R_f}{R}$. Input resistance $R_{in} = \infty$, output resistance $R_{out} = 0$.

theory.title: Differential stage
theory.body: With $R_3 = R_1$ and $R_4 = R_2$: $v_o = \frac{R_2}{R_1}(v_2 - v_1)$ — the stage amplifies the difference of the two inputs.

theory.title: Inverting summer
theory.body: $v_o = -\left(\frac{R_f}{R_1}v_1 + \frac{R_f}{R_2}v_2 + \dots + \frac{R_f}{R_n}v_n\right)$ — obtained by superposition and the result for the inverting stage (the input currents add at the virtual ground).

theory.title: Buffer (voltage follower)
theory.body: Output connected directly to the inverting input: $v_o = v_i$, $R_{in} = \infty$. It isolates a source with internal resistance $R_S$ from the load: no current is drawn from the source, so $v_L = v_S$.

theory.title: Cascaded stages
theory.body: Because an ideal stage behaves as a voltage source, stages can be cascaded: the output of one stage is the input of the next, and the overall gain is the product of the stage gains (the output does not depend on the load).

theory.title: Capacitor
theory.body: An ideal two-terminal element that stores **charge**: $q(t) = Cv(t)$. The **capacitance** $C$ is measured in farads (F), $1\ \text{F} = 1\ \text{C/V}$. With the passive sign convention, $i(t) = \frac{dq}{dt} = C\frac{dv}{dt}$.

theory.title: Parallel-plate capacitor
theory.body:
$C = \varepsilon\frac{A}{d}$ — plate area $A$, separation $d$, permittivity $\varepsilon$ (in free space $\varepsilon_0 \approx 8.854\times10^{-12}$ F/m).
- A 1-F capacitor with plates 1 m apart would need plates of about $336\ \text{km}\times336\ \text{km}$ — real capacitors are μF, nF, pF ($1\ \mu\text{F} = 10^{-6}$ F, $1$ nF $= 10^{-9}$ F, $1$ pF $= 10^{-12}$ F, $1$ fF $= 10^{-15}$ F).
- Scaled values (1 F, 2 F, ½ F) are often used for demonstration.

theory.title: Memory
theory.body: $v(t) = \frac1C\int_{-\infty}^{t}i(\tau)\,d\tau$: the voltage depends on the whole history of the current. **The voltage $v$ is the state variable of the capacitor**; initial conditions are needed: $v(t) = v(t_0) + \frac1C\int_{t_0}^{t}i\,d\tau$.

theory.title: Continuity
theory.body: **The voltage of a capacitor cannot change instantaneously.** If the current remains bounded in a closed interval $[t_1, t_2]$, the voltage is a continuous function in $(t_1, t_2)$. Example: a $\pm10$ A square-wave current into $5$ F gives a continuous triangular voltage between $0$ and $2$ V.

theory.title: Energy
theory.body:
$p = vi = Cv\frac{dv}{dt}$; energy absorbed in $[t_1, t_2]$: $w = C\int_{t_1}^{t_2}v\frac{dv}{d\tau}d\tau = \frac12Cv^2(t_2) - \frac12Cv^2(t_1)$.
**Stored energy:** $E_C(t) = \frac12Cv^2(t)$ — it depends on the present voltage only and is always $\ge 0$; the energy follows the state variable $v$.

theory.title: Series and parallel capacitors
theory.body: **Parallel:** $C_{eq} = C_1 + C_2 + \dots + C_n$ — capacitors in parallel combine like resistors in series. **Series:** $\frac{1}{C_{eq}} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \dots + \frac{1}{C_n}$ (with $v(t_0) = v_1(t_0) + \dots + v_n(t_0)$) — capacitors in series combine like resistors in parallel.

theory.title: Inductor
theory.body: An ideal two-terminal element that stores **magnetic flux**: $\psi(t) = Li(t)$, flux in webers (Wb). The **inductance** $L$ is measured in henries (H), $1\ \text{H} = 1\ \text{Wb/A}$. Then $v(t) = \frac{d\psi}{dt} = L\frac{di}{dt}$.

theory.title: Toroidal inductor
theory.body: From Faraday's and Ampère's laws, for $N$ turns on a toroid of cross-section $A$, mean circumference $l$ and relative permeability $\mu_r$: $L \simeq 4\pi\times10^{-7}\mu_r\frac{N^2A}{l}$ H. Orders of magnitude: mH, μH, nH; scaled values (1 H, 2 H, ½ H) for demonstration.

theory.title: Memory and continuity
theory.body: $i(t) = \frac1L\int_{-\infty}^{t}v(\tau)\,d\tau$: **the current $i$ is the state variable of the inductor**; initial conditions are needed. **The current through an inductor cannot change instantaneously**: if the voltage remains bounded in $[t_1, t_2]$, the current is continuous in $(t_1, t_2)$.

theory.title: Energy
theory.body: $p = vi = Li\frac{di}{dt}$; $w = \frac12Li^2(t_2) - \frac12Li^2(t_1)$. **Stored energy:** $E_L(t) = \frac12Li^2(t)$ — depends on the present current only, always $\ge 0$ (passivity).

theory.title: Series and parallel inductors
theory.body: **Series:** $L_{eq} = L_1 + L_2 + \dots + L_n$ — like resistors in series. **Parallel:** $\frac{1}{L_{eq}} = \frac{1}{L_1} + \dots + \frac{1}{L_n}$ (with $i(t_0) = i_1(t_0) + \dots + i_n(t_0)$) — like resistors in parallel.

theory.title: DC steady state
theory.body:
With constant (DC) quantities the derivatives are zero:
- **Capacitor:** $i = C\frac{dV_C}{dt} = 0$ — it behaves as an **open circuit**.
- **Inductor:** $v = L\frac{dI_L}{dt} = 0$ — it behaves as a **short circuit**.

theory.title: Objective and equipment
theory.body: Objective: be able to measure resistance, voltage and current. Equipment: power supply, digital multimeter (DMM), breadboard, resistors.

theory.title: Breadboard
theory.body: A breadboard has two internal connections. The **vertical** rails are connected from top to bottom: 5 V on the first pin is present on every pin of that rail. The **horizontal** strips connect groups of 5 pins: pins A1–E1 are joined internally.

theory.title: Digital multimeter
theory.body:
Parts: power button; 10 A jack (not used in this course); voltage jack (red lead, positive); display; range selector; measurement type (V, A, Ω); AC/DC button; **COM** jack (always used, black lead); 2 A jack (red lead for current measurements).

**Choosing the range:** select the next range above the expected value — $1.1\ \text{k}\Omega \to$ «2K», $6$ V $\to$ «20», $1$ mA $\to$ «2m».

theory.title: Power supply
theory.body: The «+6V» knob sets the 6-V output when the «+6V» meter button is pressed; the «±20V» knob sets the ±20-V outputs. The output terminals are always active while the supply is on, whatever meter button is selected — so set the voltage first, switch off, then connect the circuit.

theory.title: How to measure (good lab practice)
theory.body:
- **Resistance:** measure the resistor alone (out of the circuit, supply off).
- **Voltage:** the DMM is connected **in parallel** with the element.
- **Current:** switch the supply off, **break the circuit** and insert the DMM **in series** (positive lead toward $R_1$, negative toward $R_2$), then switch on.

theory.title: Theory and preliminary calculations
theory.body: Ohm's law in three forms: $V = IR$, $I = \frac VR$, $R = \frac VI$. Series resistors add. Figure 1.8: $6$ V, $R_1 = 1.1\ \text{k}\Omega$, $R_2 = 3.3\ \text{k}\Omega$; Figure 1.9: the same resistors with $10$ V. Compute $R_T$, $V_1$, $V_2$ and $I$ before the lab, then compare with the measurements (percent error).

theory.title: Theory
theory.body:
- KVL: the algebraic sum of the voltages around any closed path is zero, $\sum v_i = 0$; KCL: the algebraic sum of the currents at any node is zero, $\sum i_i = 0$.
- Series circuit: same current through each element, different voltages; $R_T = R_1 + \dots + R_N$ and $V_S = V_1 + \dots + V_N$.
- Parallel circuit: same voltage across each branch, different currents; $\frac{1}{R_T} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \dots + \frac{1}{R_N}$ and $I_P = I_1 + \dots + I_N$.

theory.title: Percent error
theory.body: $\text{Percent error} = \frac{\text{Measured} - \text{Theoretical}}{\text{Theoretical}}\times100$. Compare every measured value ($R$, $V$, $I$) with the calculated one; a negative value means the measurement is below the theory; the magnitude is often reported.
